newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union cancels sick pay clauses in region.
newsitem.headline: German union cancels sick pay clauses in region.

text.p: German metal and engineering trade union IG Metall said on Tuesday its branch in the steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia would be cancelling clauses in worker contracts governing sick pay.

The widely-expected move, which follows the collapse of talks on proposed cuts to sick pay entitlements by employers, will allow the some 850,000 metal and engineering workers in the sector to strike on the issue later next year.
Strikes in the sector are legally possible a month after the cancellation of wage agreements. As a result, North Rhine-Westphalia strikes will not be possible until August.

Metal and engineering workers in in the southern state of Bavaria have already said they plan to cancel wage agreements on sick pay from the end of January, allowing them to hold strikes from March onwards.
The dispute follows a new law cutting worker sick pay entitlements from 100 percent to 80 percent, which has already triggered nationwide protests by metal and engineering workers.
The talks in North Rhine-Westphalia was the latest of three high-profile efforts to resolve the dispute on wages and labour costs that has followed the passing of the sick pay law.
But industrial relations in the sector have slumped to an almost unprecedented low after a number of firms tried unsuccessfully to implement the new law without union consent.

Talks since then have focused on ways to secure the envisaged cost savings from the new law , which are estimated at up to 12 billion marks across all German industry, without directly cutting sick pay entitlements.

Previous negotiations had broken down as the two sides have not been able to agree a system under which sick pay would be maintained at 100 percent of salary in return for cuts to holiday entitlements.

Talks in North Rhine-Westphalia had been based on an entirely new approach under which low overall absenteeism in a company would be rewarded by higher end-of-year bonuses, while high sickness rates would mean lower bonuses.
Employers said they could not agree to such a scheme as it would be unworkable in practice.
